text: Question: A client has Diabetes Insipidus. Which nursing intervention is essential for monitoring this condition?
A. Inserting a Foley catheter
B. Measuring intake and output
C. Analyzing blood glucose levels
D. Sending a urine specimen to the lab
Correct answer: B. Measuring intake and output
Topic: Endocrine & Metabolic
notes: Rationale:
Correct: Diabetes insipidus causes very large volumes of dilute urine (2–20 L a day), so measuring intake and output is essential, along with daily weights.
Not correct: A Foley is not routinely needed, and blood glucose is not the problem; diabetes insipidus is unrelated to diabetes mellitus.
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 8.)
(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.)

slides.title: The nurse is caring for a client who has syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic
text: Question: The nurse is caring for a client who has syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH).  Which of the following assessment findings would indicate that the client is developing a complication?
A. A weight loss of 3 pounds in 4 days
B. Observance of neck vein distention
C. A decrease in blood pressure
D. An increase in urine output
Correct answer: B. Observance of neck vein distention
Topic: Endocrine & Metabolic
notes: Rationale:
Correct: In SIADH the body retains water, so neck vein distention is a sign of fluid overload.
Not correct: Weight loss, lower blood pressure and increased urine output are not expected with water retention (SIADH gives low urine output, weight gain and low serum sodium).
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 9.)
(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.)

text: Question: The nurse is assessing a client who has possible Cushing’s syndrome.  The nurse expects to find:
A. hypotension.
B. thick, coarse skin.
C. truncal obesity.
D. weight gain in arms and legs.
Correct answer: C. truncal obesity.
Topic: Endocrine & Metabolic
notes: Rationale:
Correct: Cushing's syndrome causes truncal obesity (with thin arms and legs), a rounded face, hypertension, muscle wasting and carbohydrate intolerance.
Not correct: Hypotension is seen in Addison's disease; thick, coarse skin in hypothyroidism; and the extremities are thin, not heavy, in Cushing's.
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 17.)
(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.)

slides.title: A nurse is educating on blood sugar control to the client who has uncontrolled d
text: Question: A nurse is educating on blood sugar control to the client who has uncontrolled diabetes that their vision may be impaired from:
A. Prolonged periods of hyperglycemia
B. Frequent injections of regular insulin
C. Lens opacity
D. Corneal dryness
Correct answer: A. Prolonged periods of hyperglycemia
Topic: Endocrine & Metabolic
notes: Rationale:
Correct: Prolonged hyperglycemia damages the small vessels of the retina (diabetic retinopathy) and can change the lens, impairing vision. Good glucose control protects the eyes.
Not correct: Insulin injections do not cause vision problems; lens opacity (cataract) and corneal dryness are not the effect of high blood glucose being taught here.
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 22.)
(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.)

slides.title: Hemoglobin A1C provides information on glucose control over the past:
text: Question: Hemoglobin A1C provides information on glucose control over the past:
A. 20 to 40 days
B. 50 to 65 days
C. 60 to 85 days
D. 90-120 days
Correct answer: D. 90-120 days
Topic: Endocrine & Metabolic
notes: Rationale:
Correct: The hemoglobin A1C reflects average glucose control over about 90–120 days (roughly 3 months), the life span of red blood cells.
Not correct: The shorter time frames are too short.
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 23.)
(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.)

slides.title: The nurse is caring for a client who has pheochromocytoma. Which of the followin
text: Question: The nurse is caring for a client who has pheochromocytoma.  Which of the following is the nurse most likely to assess?
A. Constricted pupils
B. Blood glucose level of 130 mg/dl
C. Bradycardia
D. Blood pressure of 176/88 mm Hg
Correct answer: D. Blood pressure of 176/88 mm Hg
Topic: Endocrine & Metabolic
notes: Rationale:
Correct: A pheochromocytoma releases excess catecholamines, causing hypertension (176/88 mm Hg), tachycardia, headache, sweating and anxiety.
Not correct: Constricted pupils and bradycardia are the opposite effects, and a glucose of 130 mg/dL is not a key finding.
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 25.)
(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.)

slides.title: The nurse is teaching a client who has diabetes mellitus (type 2) and a prescrip
text: Question: The nurse is teaching a client who has diabetes mellitus (type 2) and a prescription for extended-release metformin. Select 2 statements the nurse should make.
A. “You may chew the tablet if you experience any difficulty swallowing.”
B. “You need to carry emergency identification and a glucagon kit at all times.”
C. “You should contact the physician if you notice the metformin tablet in the stool.”
D. “You will need to discontinue the medication for any procedure that requires a contrast agent.”
Correct answers: B. “You need to carry emergency identification and a glucagon kit at all times.”; D. “You will need to discontinue the medication for any procedure that requires a contrast agent.”
Topic: Pharmacology & Labs
notes: Rationale:
Correct:
• “You will need to discontinue the medication for any procedure that requires a contrast agent.” – Metformin is held around contrast because of kidney injury and lactic acidosis risk.
• “You need to carry emergency identification and a glucagon kit…” – the likely intended second answer for this select-two item.
Not correct:
• Extended-release tablets must be swallowed whole, never chewed.
• The empty tablet shell can appear in the stool and is harmless; there is no need to call.
(From your class slides: Endocrine, slide 26.)

(Answer key not on the slide; worked out with NCLEX reasoning, so check it against your class notes.) The glucagon-kit option is the least certain part of this key (metformin alone rarely causes low blood sugar).
